## Start with the unit's own status

Before touching configuration, run `systemctl status <service>` and read the last several log lines it prints inline. Most failures fall into one of a few buckets: the binary path is wrong, a dependency hasn't started yet, a config file has a syntax error, or the process is crashing immediately after start.

## Read the full journal, not just the summary

`systemctl status` truncates. Pull the complete picture with:

```bash
journalctl -u <service> --since "10 min ago"
```

Look for the first error in the sequence, not the last — cascading failures often bury the real cause under several follow-on errors.

## Check dependency ordering

A service that "sometimes" fails on boot is often a `Wants=`/`After=` ordering problem rather than a bug in the service itself. Confirm the unit file's dependencies actually match what the service needs to be available (network, a mounted filesystem, another service) before assuming the code is at fault.

## Validate the environment, not just the unit file

Services run under systemd often have a different `PATH`, working directory, and environment than the same command run interactively as a user. If something "works when I run it myself" but fails under systemd, diff the environment first — an `Environment=` audit usually finds it faster than re-reading the same unit file a fourth time.

## Keep a personal log of root causes

Over time, patterns repeat: a missing `After=network-online.target`, a relative path that only works from one working directory, a permissions mismatch after a package upgrade. Keeping a short personal note of "what it turned out to be" for each incident makes the next one faster to diagnose.
